extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, and critics interested in principles of honest materials and ornamentation
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for the lawful and honest use of materials, ornament, painting, and machine-work in architecture, with guidance and examples of acceptable vs. deceptive practices. Emphasises dignity, permanence, and the moral/aesthetic value of truthful construction and ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect historical/material precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Every idea respecting size, proportion, decoration, or construction depends on presupposition of traditional materials; true architecture should retain, as far as possible, the materials and principles of earlier ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture historically developed from readily accessible materials (clay, wood, stone); even with advanced technology, designers should be cautious about departing from those first principles because the historical use gives architecture dignity and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture does not admit iron as a constructive material
rubrics_metrics.description: True architecture does not admit iron as a constructive material; metallic constructions (iron roofs, cast-iron spires) are not architecture in the proper sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metals may appear in buildings (nails, rivets, supports for statues) but should not replace stone/wood in bearing or act as principal structural elements; examples allowed include rivets, chains around domes, or iron bars supporting statues, provided they do not take the place of masonry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metals may be used as cement, not as supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals may be used as a cement but not as a support — they may perform functions analogous to strong cement but must not bear weight in the manner of stone or wood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: metal rods or rivets can be used in place of cement where they merely prevent separation of stones; the use is lawful if the metal's role could, in principle, be superseded by sufficient cement. If iron takes the place of stone or wood-beams (bearing weight or replacing buttresses), the work ceases to be true architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extravagant or frequent use of metal
rubrics_metrics.description: Even within permissible limits, extravagant or frequent employment of metal derogates from the dignity and honesty of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectators assume separable stones; overuse of iron conceals masonry skill and reduces the perceived mastery of the architect. Use metal sparingly and only where necessary; do not allow reliance on iron to excuse poor masonry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer stone-fitting and good mortar before resorting to metal
rubrics_metrics.description: When mortar needs assistance, the dovetailing and adjusting of stones should be attempted before introducing metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stone may be cut and shaped into complex forms (fitting in any shape the architect pleases) to aid mortar; these honest artifices are preferable to metal fixes. Avoid introducing principal stones in apparently impossible positions unless clearly an admitted help or an unimportant decorative riddle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary restraints and obedience to natural laws are virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Highest greatness is shown by noble submission to constraints; architects should accept voluntary restrictions (material limits) rather than infringing natural laws for apparent advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with natural creation: order and system are nobler than brute power. Architects should prefer design solutions that respect chosen material laws even if more difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface deceits (painting to represent nonexistent material) are condemnable
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface deceits are inducing the supposition of some form or material which does not actually exist (e.g., painting wood to represent marble); the evil lies in definite attempted deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gross examples (roof of Milan Cathedral painted to look like elaborate tracery) are strongly reprehended; such practices destroy dignity. Painting that knowingly tries to pass for real material is base and inadmissible in architecture of high rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting is legitimate when confessed as painting or integrated with subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting, when clearly painting (not asserting any material), is not deception and is legitimate; if the sense of paint remains, it may enrich a surface without falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sistine Chapel's painted architecture is acceptable because it is integrated with figures and clearly painted; a fresco with a flat border (Campo Santo at Pisa) secures certainty of flat surface and avoids deception. Exception: where subject or artist's authority precludes deception (e.g., a dome painted as heavenly opening), the illusion may be permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trompe-l'oeil in decorative contexts may be tolerated as 'toys' but not as architectural truth
rubrics_metrics.description: In rooms, villas, gardens, or places meant for idleness, pictured landscapes or ceilings like skies can be fitting admissions of trickery as innocent amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such trickeries are allowable when regarded consciously as playthings and not as serious architectural declaration of material or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: False representation of material is base and inadmissible
rubrics_metrics.description: All such imitations (marbling, mosaic imitations, powdering with lapis lazuli, painted stucco made to look like alabaster) are utterly base and inadmissible in architecture of higher rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites wasted expense on shop-front marbling and imitation marble landing in the British Museum as examples that cast suspicion on surrounding real stones; avoid imitative finishes that pretend to be other materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church furniture and sacred spaces should be simple and unaffected
rubrics_metrics.description: The first condition required in church furniture is that it should be simple and unaffected, not fictitious nor tawdry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid painted iron, faux-marble, gaudy upholstery, and other disguises in places of worship that hinder devotional feeling; prefer solid stone and wood, whitewashed if necessary for cleanliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment that does not assert falsehood is allowable (whitewash, gilding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealment (whitewash) or thin surface treatments that do not pretend to be what they are (gilding as a film) are not falsehoods and may be permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitewash shows itself and asserts nothing beneath; gilding, while often abused, is acceptable when used with respect to express magnificence or sacredness, not as sign-painting or vulgar vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veneering with precious stone is permissible if not pretending to be solid
rubrics_metrics.description: Facing brick with thin slabs of precious stone (veneer) is allowable provided it does not pretend or imply a solid stone wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such veneering is effectively a large-scale mosaic and often necessary where obtaining mass of precious stone is impossible; designers should be honest about veneering and weigh sacrifice and truth (substance vs ornament).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure enduring, substantial construction before applying ephemeral decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting and external coloring divide the work into two parts of differing durability; secure the lasting 'noblesse' of solid construction before resorting to decorative painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural stone colors and durable materials; reserve painter's work for interiors and loggias; use glass and gold in mosaic when brighter color is required because mosaic is as durable as solid stone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative deceit: machine or cast work masquerading as hand-work is dishonest
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting cast or machine work for hand-work is both bad as workmanship and dishonest as an imposition pretending to human labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament's second source of value is the sense of human labor; false ornaments that pretend to cost or care they did not have are an imposition, vulgarity, and sin. Reject machine-cast ornament used to simulate hand-carving; prefer genuine hand-work or openly machine-made forms that do not pretend otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for materials like brick, tile, porcelain, terra cotta when honest
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials known to be moulded (brick, tile, porcelain) can legitimately be cast and used in elaborate decoration because they do not pretend to be cut stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: brick mouldings of Italian palazzi, colored tiles in French domestic architecture, terra cotta bas-reliefs by the Della Robbia family — these are acceptable and may even require great skill. Human-wrought terra cotta or plaster is worth more than machine-cut stone if the human labor is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true hand-work from machine-like hand-work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible for hand-work to carry the characters of mechanism; the value of ornament depends on the consciousness of human labour, not merely on form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers and patrons should favor work that visibly bears the record of thought, trial, and care; avoid processes where even 'hand-work' has been reduced to mechanical sameness and thereby loses the intrinsic worth derived from human labour.
